prompt: Table sugar is a molecular compound, and potassium chloride, KCl, is an ionic compound. Both dissolve in water. Which statement correctly describes what happens to each?

choices.text: Sugar molecules drift apart from each other; KCl separates into K^+ and Cl^− ions
Sugar and KCl both separate into positive and negative ions
choices.why: Only ionic compounds separate into ions. Sugar is molecular, so its molecules simply drift apart from each other.

choices.text: Sugar separates into ions; KCl units drift apart from each other intact
choices.why: This has the two reversed. The ions of an ionic compound separate, while the molecules of a molecular compound stay whole.

choices.text: Sugar breaks into C, H, and O atoms; KCl breaks into K and Cl atoms
choices.why: Neither compound breaks into neutral atoms. Sugar molecules stay whole, and KCl separates into charged ions, not atoms.

explanation: When a molecular compound such as sugar dissolves, its individual molecules drift apart from each other. When an ionic compound dissolves, the ions themselves physically separate, so KCl becomes K^+(aq) and Cl^−(aq).

prompt: When an ionic compound dissolves in water, its ions separate from each other and go their own way in solution. What is this process called?

choices.why: Precipitation is nearly the opposite: dissolved ions come together to form a solid that falls out of solution.
A double-replacement reaction exchanges ions between two compounds. Dissolving involves one compound, and its ions stay the same ions.
In a single-replacement reaction, an element takes the place of another element in a compound. No element takes part when a compound simply dissolves.

explanation: The separation of an ionic compound into its ions as it dissolves is called dissociation; we say the ions dissociate. The (aq) label on each ion shows that it is dissolved.

prompt: In his 1884 PhD dissertation, the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius proposed that ionic compounds separate into ions when they dissolve. How was this idea received?

choices.text: His examiners doubted it and barely passed him; it was later cited for his Nobel Prize
His examiners praised it at once, and he won the Nobel Prize for it that same year
choices.why: His examiners had a hard time believing the idea. The recognition came later, when the work was cited for his Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

choices.text: His examiners rejected it, and the idea was forgotten until long after his death
choices.why: The idea was not forgotten. Arrhenius passed, and this work was later cited when he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

choices.text: His examiners failed him, so he never completed his PhD or did further research
choices.why: Arrhenius did pass, though with a barely passing grade, and he went on to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

explanation: Arrhenius's examiners had a hard time believing that ionic compounds would behave this way and gave him a barely passing grade. Later, this work was cited when he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

prompt: Iron(III) sulfate, Fe2(SO4)3, dissolves in water. Which equation correctly represents this process?

choices.why: The two iron ions and the three sulfate ions all separate from one another. The subscripts become coefficients showing how many of each ion form.
Sulfate is a polyatomic ion, and polyatomic ions keep their identity when they dissolve. It stays together as SO4^2−.
Iron(III) means Fe^3+. With Fe^2+, the ions would carry 4+ and 6− in total, so the charges would not balance.

explanation: Each formula unit releases two Fe^3+ ions and three SO4^2− ions, and each sulfate ion stays intact. Check: 2(3+) + 3(2−) = 0, matching the neutral compound.

prompt: Ammonium phosphate, (NH4)3PO4, is soluble in water. How many ions in total are released into solution when one formula unit of (NH4)3PO4 dissolves?
explanation: One formula unit separates into three NH4^+ ions and one PO4^3− ion, for 4 ions in total. Both are polyatomic ions, so they stay together instead of breaking into N, H, P, and O.

prompt: A student writes the equation for magnesium bromide dissolving in water as MgBr2(s) → Mg^2+(aq) + Br2^2−(aq). What is wrong with it?

choices.text: The two bromide ions separate from each other, so it should show 2Br^−(aq)
The bromine should be written as Br2(aq), since bromine is diatomic
choices.why: Br2 is elemental bromine, a different substance. Dissolving MgBr2 produces bromide ions, Br^−, not bromine molecules.

choices.text: MgBr2 should stay whole as MgBr2(aq), since it only dissolves and does not react
choices.why: When an ionic compound dissolves, its ions physically separate even when no reaction takes place.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong, because the atoms and the charges both balance
choices.why: The atoms and charges do balance, but there is no Br2^2− ion. The two bromide ions go their own way as separate Br^− ions.

explanation: When an ionic compound dissolves, all of its ions separate: MgBr2(s) → Mg^2+(aq) + 2Br^−(aq). The bromide ions don't stay paired as Br2^2−, and they don't become elemental Br2.

prompt: In a complete ionic equation, which substances are written as separated ions?

choices.text: Ionic compounds that are dissolved in the solution
Every ionic compound, including any solid precipitate
choices.why: A precipitate is not dissolved, so its ions are not separated. It is written as one formula with an (s) label.

choices.text: Only the ionic compounds on the reactant side
choices.why: Dissolved products, such as a soluble salt that forms, are also written as separated ions.

choices.text: Only ionic compounds that contain polyatomic ions
choices.why: Any dissolved ionic compound is split into its ions, including simple ones such as NaCl. A polyatomic ion itself stays in one piece.

explanation: A complete ionic equation writes each dissolved ionic compound, reactant or product, as its separated ions, because that is how it exists in solution. A solid, such as a precipitate, keeps its whole formula.

prompt: Solutions of sodium carbonate and magnesium chloride react: Na2CO3(aq) + MgCl2(aq) → MgCO3(s) + 2NaCl(aq). Which is the complete ionic equation for this reaction?

choices.why: MgCO3 is a solid precipitate, not a dissolved compound, so it is written as MgCO3(s) rather than as ions.

choices.text: Na^+(aq) + CO3^2−(aq) + Mg^2+(aq) + Cl^−(aq) → MgCO3(s) + Na^+(aq) + Cl^−(aq)
choices.why: The ion counts are missing: Na2CO3 releases two Na^+ ions, MgCl2 releases two Cl^− ions, and 2NaCl gives two of each.
NaCl is dissolved, as its (aq) label shows, so it must also be written as separated Na^+ and Cl^− ions.

explanation: Na2CO3 gives 2Na^+ + CO3^2−, MgCl2 gives Mg^2+ + 2Cl^−, and 2NaCl gives 2Na^+ + 2Cl^−, while the precipitate stays together as MgCO3(s). Getting the counts right means turning each subscript and coefficient into a number of ions.

prompt: Solutions of strontium hydroxide, Sr(OH)2, and nickel(II) nitrate, Ni(NO3)2, are mixed, and a double-replacement reaction occurs. In the complete ionic equation, which substance is written as a whole formula with an (s) label instead of as separate ions?

choices.why: Most hydroxides are insoluble, but Sr^2+ is one of the exceptions. Sr(OH)2 is dissolved, so it is written as Sr^2+ and OH^− ions.
Compounds of the nitrate ion are soluble with no exceptions, so this product stays dissolved and is written as Sr^2+ and NO3^− ions.
This is one of the dissolved reactants. As a nitrate compound it is soluble, so it is written as Ni^2+ and NO3^− ions.

explanation: The possible products are Ni(OH)2 and Sr(NO3)2. Hydroxides are insoluble unless the cation is one of the exceptions, and Ni^2+ is not, so Ni(OH)2 precipitates and is written as Ni(OH)2(s). Every other substance is dissolved and is written as ions.

prompt: For the reaction Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq), a student writes this complete ionic equation: Pb^2+(aq) + 2NO3^−(aq) + 2K^+(aq) + 2I^−(aq) → Pb^2+(aq) + 2I^−(aq) + 2K^+(aq) + 2NO3^−(aq). What did the student do wrong?

choices.text: Wrote the solid PbI2 as separated ions instead of as PbI2(s)
Included the K^+ and NO3^− ions, which don't belong in a complete ionic equation
choices.why: A complete ionic equation shows every dissolved ion, including ones that don't change. They are removed only when you go on to write the net ionic equation.

choices.text: Wrote the two iodide ions separately instead of as one I2 unit
choices.why: I2 is elemental iodine. Dissolved iodide ions are separate I^− ions, so 2I^−(aq) is correct on the reactant side.

choices.text: Kept nitrate together as NO3^− instead of splitting it into N and O
choices.why: Nitrate is a polyatomic ion, and polyatomic ions keep their identity in solution, so NO3^− is correct.

explanation: PbI2 is insoluble (Pb^2+ is an exception for iodide compounds), so it is a solid and keeps its whole formula: the product side should be PbI2(s) + 2K^+(aq) + 2NO3^−(aq). As the student wrote it, nothing changes at all from one side to the other.

prompt: The reaction Zn(NO3)2(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → Zn(OH)2(s) + 2KNO3(aq) is rewritten as a complete ionic equation. Counting each ion as many times as its coefficient shows, how many separate ions are written in the complete ionic equation, on both sides together?
explanation: Reactant side: Zn^2+ + 2NO3^− + 2K^+ + 2OH^− = 7 ions. Product side: Zn(OH)2(s) stays together as a solid, plus 2K^+ + 2NO3^− = 4 ions. Total: 7 + 4 = 11.

prompt: What is a spectator ion?

choices.text: An ion that is present but does not take part in the overall chemical change
An ion that combines with another ion to form the solid precipitate
choices.why: Ions that form the precipitate change from dissolved ions into a solid, so they do take part in the reaction.

choices.text: An ion that appears only on the reactant side of an ionic equation
choices.why: A spectator ion appears on both sides of the complete ionic equation in exactly the same form, because it does not change.

choices.text: An ion whose charge changes during the course of the reaction
choices.why: A spectator ion does not change at all; it has the same formula, charge, and (aq) label on both sides.

explanation: Spectator ions are present in the solution but do nothing in the overall course of the reaction. They appear unchanged on both sides of a complete ionic equation, so they can be canceled.

prompt: Solutions of strontium chloride and lithium sulfate are mixed: SrCl2(aq) + Li2SO4(aq) → SrSO4(s) + 2LiCl(aq). After the solid forms, where are the Li^+ ions?

choices.text: Still dissolved in the solution, unchanged

choices.why: The precipitate is SrSO4, which is made of Sr^2+ and SO4^2− ions only. Li^+ does not become part of it.

choices.text: Combined with chloride ions as solid LiCl
choices.why: All lithium compounds are soluble, so LiCl stays dissolved as separate Li^+ and Cl^− ions.

choices.text: Removed from the beaker when they are canceled
choices.why: Canceling spectator ions happens only on paper, when writing the net ionic equation. The ions are still in the solution.

explanation: Li^+ starts as Li^+(aq) and ends as Li^+(aq), so it is a spectator ion. Spectator ions remain in the solution after the reaction; they simply aren't written in the net ionic equation.

prompt: Solutions of lead(II) acetate and ammonium sulfate react: Pb(C2H3O2)2(aq) + (NH4)2SO4(aq) → PbSO4(s) + 2NH4C2H3O2(aq). Which ions are the spectator ions?

choices.why: These ions combine to form the PbSO4 precipitate, so they take part in the reaction.
NH4^+ is a spectator, but SO4^2− ends up in the solid PbSO4.
Acetate is a spectator, but Pb^2+ ends up in the solid PbSO4.

explanation: In the complete ionic equation, NH4^+(aq) and C2H3O2^−(aq) appear unchanged on both sides, so they are the spectators. Pb^2+ and SO4^2− leave the solution as PbSO4(s).

prompt: Consider the reaction Al2(SO4)3(aq) + 3Ba(NO3)2(aq) → 3BaSO4(s) + 2Al(NO3)3(aq). In its complete ionic equation, how many spectator ions appear on the reactant side, counting each ion as many times as its coefficient shows?
explanation: The reactant side is 2Al^3+ + 3SO4^2− + 3Ba^2+ + 6NO3^−. Ba^2+ and SO4^2− form BaSO4(s), while 2Al^3+ and 6NO3^− appear unchanged on the product side. So the spectators on the reactant side number 2 + 6 = 8.

prompt: Here is a complete ionic equation: Ca^2+(aq) + 2NO3^−(aq) + 2Na^+(aq) + CO3^2−(aq) → CaCO3(s) + 2Na^+(aq) + 2NO3^−(aq). A student says calcium is a spectator because calcium appears on both sides. Is the student right?

choices.text: No; calcium goes from dissolved Ca^2+ ions into solid CaCO3, so it takes part
Yes; any element that appears on both sides of an equation is a spectator
choices.why: Every element appears on both sides of a balanced equation. A spectator must appear in exactly the same form, as the same dissolved ion, on both sides.

choices.text: Yes; cations are always spectators, and only anions form the precipitate
choices.why: Every precipitate contains both a cation and an anion; CaCO3 is made of Ca^2+ and CO3^2− ions.

choices.text: No; only polyatomic ions such as NO3^− can ever be spectator ions
choices.why: Monatomic ions can be spectators too: Na^+ is a spectator in this very reaction.

explanation: Calcium is Ca^2+(aq) on the left but part of CaCO3(s) on the right, so it changes. The spectators are Na^+ and NO3^−, which are unchanged on both sides, and the net ionic equation is Ca^2+(aq) + CO3^2−(aq) → CaCO3(s).

prompt: Solutions of sodium sulfate, Na2SO4, and magnesium chloride, MgCl2, are mixed. What is the net ionic equation?

choices.text: There is none, because every ion is a spectator and no reaction occurs

choices.why: MgSO4 is soluble: sulfates generally dissolve, and magnesium is not one of the exceptions.
All sodium compounds are soluble, so NaCl stays dissolved as separate ions.

choices.text: There is none, because sodium sulfate does not separate into ions in water
choices.why: Na2SO4 is soluble, so it does separate into ions when it dissolves. The real reason is that neither possible product is insoluble.

explanation: The possible products, NaCl and MgSO4, are both soluble, so no precipitate forms. Every ion would appear unchanged on both sides of the complete ionic equation, all of them cancel, and no reaction is expected.

prompt: According to the solubility rules, which ion will be a spectator ion in every precipitation reaction in which it is present?

choices.why: Silver compounds of Cl^−, Br^−, and I^− are insoluble, so Ag^+ often ends up in the precipitate.
Barium sulfate is insoluble, so Ba^2+ becomes part of the precipitate when it meets sulfate ions.
Most hydroxides are insoluble, so OH^− often ends up in the precipitate.

explanation: All compounds of K^+ are soluble, with no exceptions, so K^+ can never end up in a precipitate. It stays dissolved and unchanged, which makes it a spectator ion.

prompt: What does a net ionic equation show?

choices.text: Only the ions and other substances that change during the reaction
Every ion in the solution, including ions that stay the same
choices.why: Spectator ions are canceled when writing a net ionic equation, so it does not show every ion present.

choices.text: Every reactant and product written as a complete formula
choices.why: In a net ionic equation, the dissolved ions that react are written as separate ions, not as complete formulas of their compounds.

choices.text: Only the solid precipitate that forms during the reaction
choices.why: A net ionic equation also shows, as reactants, the dissolved ions that come together to form the precipitate.

explanation: A net ionic equation is what remains after the spectator ions are canceled from the complete ionic equation. It represents the actual chemical change taking place.

prompt: Here is the complete ionic equation for a reaction: Cu^2+(aq) + SO4^2−(aq) + 2Na^+(aq) + 2OH^−(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s) + 2Na^+(aq) + SO4^2−(aq). What is the net ionic equation?

choices.why: Na^+ and SO4^2− are the ions that stay unchanged; they are the ones to cancel, not to keep.
Cu(OH)2 contains two OH groups, so two OH^− ions are needed. As written, neither the atoms nor the charges balance.
SO4^2− appears unchanged on both sides, so it should also be canceled.

explanation: Na^+ and SO4^2− appear unchanged on both sides, so they cancel. What remains is Cu^2+(aq) + 2OH^−(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s), which balances in both atoms and charge (2+ and 2− make 0).

prompt: Silver nitrate and sodium carbonate solutions react: 2AgNO3(aq) + Na2CO3(aq) → Ag2CO3(s) + 2NaNO3(aq). Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.why: There is no Ag2^2+ ion. The two silver ions come from two separate AgNO3 units and are written as 2Ag^+.
This has one silver atom on the left and two on the right, and the charges (1− on the left, 0 on the right) don't balance either.
Na^+ and NO3^− stay dissolved and unchanged throughout, so they are canceled, not kept.

explanation: Writing the dissolved compounds as ions gives 2Ag^+ + 2NO3^− + 2Na^+ + CO3^2− → Ag2CO3(s) + 2Na^+ + 2NO3^−. Canceling Na^+ and NO3^− leaves 2Ag^+(aq) + CO3^2−(aq) → Ag2CO3(s).

prompt: Solutions of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, and sodium phosphate, Na3PO4, are mixed, and a precipitate forms. Write the net ionic equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of PO4^3−(aq)?
explanation: Calcium phosphate is insoluble, so the precipitate is Ca3(PO4)2, while Na^+ and NO3^− are spectators. The net ionic equation is 3Ca^2+(aq) + 2PO4^3−(aq) → Ca3(PO4)2(s), and the charges check: 3(2+) + 2(3−) = 0.

prompt: The reaction BaCl2(aq) + K2CO3(aq) → BaCO3(s) + 2KCl(aq) has a certain net ionic equation. Which other reaction has exactly the same net ionic equation?

choices.why: The precipitate here is BaSO4, so its net ionic equation involves SO4^2− instead of CO3^2−.
The precipitate here is CaCO3, so its net ionic equation involves Ca^2+ instead of Ba^2+.
Barium stays dissolved in this reaction and is a spectator. The precipitate is AgCl, so the net ionic equation is different.

explanation: Both reactions have the net ionic equation Ba^2+(aq) + CO3^2−(aq) → BaCO3(s). Their spectator ions differ (K^+ and Cl^− in one, Na^+ and NO3^− in the other), but spectators don't appear in a net ionic equation.

prompt: Solutions of barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2, and magnesium sulfate, MgSO4, are mixed, and a double-replacement reaction occurs. Use the solubility rules to choose the correct net ionic equation.

choices.why: Mg(OH)2 also precipitates, since magnesium is not one of the exceptions for hydroxides, so Mg^2+ and OH^− are not spectators.
BaSO4 also precipitates, since Ba^2+ is one of the exceptions for sulfates, so Ba^2+ and SO4^2− are not spectators.

choices.text: There is none, because both products are soluble and every ion is a spectator
choices.why: Both products are insoluble, so none of the ions stays unchanged.

explanation: Both possible products are insoluble: BaSO4 (Ba^2+ is a sulfate exception) and Mg(OH)2 (Mg^2+ is not a hydroxide exception). Every ion ends up in a solid, so there are no spectator ions and nothing cancels.

prompt: The reaction between lead(II) nitrate and sodium bromide solutions, which forms solid PbBr2, can be written in several ways. Which of these is the net ionic equation?

choices.why: This writes every compound as its complete formula, so it is not an ionic equation at all.
This is the complete ionic equation. Na^+ and NO3^− appear unchanged on both sides and still need to be canceled.
This only shows sodium bromide dissolving, not the reaction that forms PbBr2.

explanation: Canceling the spectator ions Na^+ and NO3^−, which appear unchanged on both sides of the complete ionic equation, leaves Pb^2+(aq) + 2Br^−(aq) → PbBr2(s).

prompt: A copper wire is placed in silver nitrate solution, and a single-replacement reaction occurs: Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) → Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s). Which is the net ionic equation?

choices.why: The atoms balance, but the charges don't: 1+ on the left and 2+ on the right. Two Ag^+ ions are needed.
NO3^− appears unchanged on both sides, so it is a spectator ion and should be canceled.
AgNO3 is dissolved, so it is written as Ag^+ and NO3^− ions, and then the nitrate ions cancel.

explanation: Writing the dissolved compounds as ions gives Cu(s) + 2Ag^+ + 2NO3^− → Cu^2+ + 2NO3^− + 2Ag(s). Canceling NO3^− leaves Cu(s) + 2Ag^+(aq) → Cu^2+(aq) + 2Ag(s), which balances both atoms and charge (2+ on each side).

prompt: Each of these is meant to be the net ionic equation for a precipitate forming from solution. Which one is correct?

choices.why: The atoms balance, but the charges don't: 2+ and 3− give 1− on the left, while the solid on the right is neutral. Fe(OH)3 forms from Fe^3+.
The atoms balance, but the charges don't: 1+ on the left and 0 on the right. A Pb^2+ ion needs two OH^− ions, giving Pb(OH)2.
The atoms and charges balance, but Ba(OH)2 is soluble (Ba^2+ is an exception for hydroxides), so it does not precipitate.

explanation: Al^3+ + 3OH^− → Al(OH)3(s) balances the atoms (1 Al, 3 O, 3 H on each side) and the charge (3+ and 3− make 0), and aluminum hydroxide is insoluble. A correct net ionic equation must balance charge as well as atoms.

prompt: At room temperature, a maximum of 36.0 g of sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water. A student stirs 50.0 g of NaCl into 100 g of room-temperature water. How many grams of NaCl remain undissolved?
explanation: Only 36.0 g can dissolve in 100 g of water, so 50.0 g − 36.0 g = 14.0 g of NaCl stays undissolved as a solid.

prompt: At room temperature, at most 36.0 g of NaCl dissolves in 100 g of water, but only 0.00019 g of AgCl does. Which statement correctly explains why AgCl is classified as insoluble?

choices.text: Solubility is a matter of degree, and AgCl dissolves too little to count as soluble
AgCl is insoluble because not even a tiny amount of it dissolves in water
choices.why: A small amount, 0.00019 g per 100 g of water, does dissolve. Insoluble compounds dissolve so little that we treat them as not dissolving.

choices.text: Any compound that dissolves less than NaCl does is classified as insoluble
choices.why: Some compounds are only moderately soluble. Only compounds that dissolve very, very little are considered insoluble.

choices.text: AgCl is insoluble because it is a molecular compound rather than an ionic one
choices.why: AgCl is ionic, made of Ag^+ and Cl^− ions. Ionic compounds range from very soluble to so slightly soluble that we call them insoluble.

explanation: Solubility versus insolubility is a matter of degree. NaCl is very soluble, while AgCl dissolves so little (0.00019 g per 100 g of water) that it is considered insoluble.

prompt: Tap water often contains a little dissolved calcium carbonate, CaCO3. Over time, a solid called limescale, made largely of CaCO3, builds up inside tank-type water heaters. Why does it form there?

choices.text: CaCO3 is less soluble in hot water than in cold water, so heating the water makes it precipitate
Cold water entering the tank holds less CaCO3 than hot water, so the solid forms as it enters
choices.why: That is true of many solids, but CaCO3 is unusual: it is less soluble in hot water, so the solid forms as the water is heated.

choices.text: Heating breaks the dissolved CaCO3 into more ions, and those ions stick to the tank walls
choices.why: Separated ions are dissolved ions. Limescale forms when Ca^2+ and CO3^2− ions come together as a solid precipitate.

choices.text: The heated water boils away in the tank and leaves all of its dissolved compounds behind
choices.why: A tank water heater stays full of water. The solid forms because hot water can hold less dissolved CaCO3 than cold water.

explanation: CaCO3 has the relatively unusual property of being less soluble in hot water than in cold water. As a water heater warms the water, CaCO3 can precipitate if there is enough of it, forming limescale.
